case.case_title: Dissanayake v. University of Sri Jayawardenapura and Two Others
case.source_citation: Sri Lanka Law Reports [1986] 2 Sri L.R. 254

case_context.legal_issue: Whether the Vice-Chancellor’s order prohibiting the petitioner from entering University premises infringed the petitioner’s fundamental right to freedom of movement under Article 14(1)(h).
case_context.petitioner_claim: The petitioner claimed that the order making University premises out of bounds violated his right to freedom of movement as guaranteed by Article 14(1)(h).
case_context.respondent_argument: The Vice-Chancellor argued that the restriction was a necessary disciplinary measure to maintain order and discipline within the University and was lawful under the Universities Act.
key_facts: Petitioner was prohibited from entering University premises by the Vice-Chancellor’s order.
The order followed charges of unauthorized publication and disruption of examinations.
The Vice-Chancellor relied on statutory authority to maintain discipline.
The petitioner claimed this restriction violated his freedom of movement.

reasoning.interpretation_summary: The Court held that freedom of movement under Article 14(1)(h) is subject to reasonable regulation, especially in the University context where discipline and order are essential. The Vice-Chancellor’s power to maintain discipline includes restricting access to premises to prevent disruption.
reasoning.application_to_facts: The Court found that the restriction on the petitioner’s movement within University premises was a lawful disciplinary measure justified by the need to maintain order and prevent disruption of examinations. Therefore, it did not constitute an unlawful infringement of the petitioner’s freedom of movement.
principles_established: Freedom of movement is not absolute and may be regulated for maintaining discipline.
University disciplinary authority includes power to restrict movement on premises to prevent disruption.
Fundamental rights must be balanced against institutional needs for order.

outcome.holding: The Court dismissed the petitioner’s claim that his freedom of movement was violated by the Vice-Chancellor’s order restricting his access to University premises.

link_explanation.why_this_clause_matters: Article 14(1)(h) was materially engaged because the petitioner challenged the Vice-Chancellor’s order restricting his physical access to University premises as a violation of his freedom of movement.

evidence.evidence_excerpt: The Court held that the Vice-Chancellor’s order restricting the petitioner’s access to University premises was a lawful disciplinary measure and did not unlawfully infringe the petitioner’s freedom of movement.
